clinicalPearls: Caused by measles virus, a paramyxovirus; transmitted primarily by respiratory droplets and, less commonly, by small-particle aerosols that can remain suspended in air, making it highly transmissible (Harrison 22e p.1639).
Incubation is ~10 days to fever onset and ~14 days to rash onset; this period may be shorter in infants and longer (up to 3 weeks) in adults (Harrison 22e p.1640).
Classic prodrome is fever and malaise beginning ~10 days after exposure, followed by the three Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, increasing in severity over ~4 days (Harrison 22e p.1640).

Koplik's spots (bluish-white ~1 mm dots surrounded by erythema on the buccal mucosa opposite the lower molars) are pathognomonic, appear ~2 days before the rash, and fade with rash onset (Harrison 22e p.1641).

The exanthem is an erythematous maculopapular rash beginning behind the ears and on the neck/hairline, spreading cephalocaudally to face, trunk, arms, and then legs/feet by the end of the second day; it fades in the same order and may desquamate, especially in undernourished children (Harrison 22e p.1641).
Care is largely supportive; vitamin A is recommended for children with measles and can markedly reduce morbidity and mortality (Harrison 22e p.1641).
Two doses of live attenuated measles vaccine (commonly as MMR or MMRV) are highly protective; ~85% develop protective antibody after one dose at 9 months and ~95% at 12 months (Harrison 22e p.1642).

Post-exposure human immunoglobulin within 72 h usually prevents infection and, given up to 6 days after exposure, can still prevent or modify disease in susceptible high-risk contacts (Harrison 22e p.1642).

Endemic transmission was eliminated in the United States in 2000, but outbreaks recur from imported cases amplified in under- and unvaccinated communities; vaccine hesitancy and pandemic-related disruption of immunization programs have driven a global resurgence (Harrison 22e p.1638, p.1369).
harrison.pathophysiology: Measles virus is deposited in the respiratory tract, oropharynx, or conjunctivae, then proliferates locally in dendritic cells and lymphocytes and spreads to draining lymph nodes. It enters the bloodstream by budding from infected lymphocytes, producing a viremia that disseminates infection throughout the body (respiratory epithelium, lymphatic tissue, spleen, lung, thymus, liver, skin). Signs and symptoms appear 8-12 days after infection as virus replicates in target organs and the host immune response develops; the characteristic rash is itself a consequence of the cellular immune response. TH1 (interferon-gamma) responses are essential for viral clearance and later TH2 (interleukin-4) responses drive protective antibody. Paradoxically, measles induces a state of immunosuppression lasting weeks to months that depresses responses to unrelated antigens, reduces the magnitude and diversity of pre-existing antibody ("immune amnesia"), and increases susceptibility to secondary bacterial and viral infections, accounting for much measles-related morbidity and death.
additionalDifferentials: Rubella (German measles) - milder, no cough, with posterior auricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy
Infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytosis, in contrast to the leukopenia common in measles)
Roseola (exanthem subitum) - rash appears after fever subsides
infectionMimics: Early meningococcemia or rickettsial infection (morbilliform before petechiae/purpura)
additionalInvestigations: Detection of measles virus-specific IgM in a single serum or oral fluid specimen is diagnostic of acute infection
Fourfold or greater rise in measles virus-specific IgG between acute- and convalescent-phase sera
Note timing pitfall: IgM may not be detectable until 4-5 days after rash onset (false-negatives if drawn too early) and usually falls to undetectable within 4-8 weeks
Reverse-transcription PCR for measles virus RNA (sensitive/specific; can genotype and distinguish wild-type from vaccine strain)
Virus isolation in cell culture from respiratory secretions, nasopharyngeal/conjunctival swabs, blood, or urine
Direct detection of giant cells in respiratory secretions, urine, or biopsy tissue
Neutralization tests (highly correlated with protective immunity but expensive and laborious)
redFlags: Pneumonia - secondary bacterial bronchopneumonia or measles giant cell pneumonitis (the latter in immunocompromised persons); recurrence or persistence of fever after the rash suggests secondary bacterial infection
Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) with risk of airway obstruction, particularly in young children
Post-measles encephalomyelitis (~1 in 1000 cases) within 2 weeks of rash onset with fever, seizures, and neurologic abnormalities - thought to be autoimmune
Measles inclusion body encephalitis (MIBE) - rare, fatal, in those with defective cellular immunity, months after infection
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) - slowly progressive, fatal, 5-15 years after infection (mostly in those infected at <2 years)
Absent or delayed rash in immunocompromised or severely undernourished children with impaired cellular immunity - associated with a high case-fatality rate
harrison.prognosis: Most persons recover and develop long-term (generally lifelong) protective immunity. Case-fatality varies with age at infection, nutritional and immunologic status, vaccine coverage, and access to care. In most developed countries the case-fatality rate is 0.01-0.1%, but in endemic areas of sub-Saharan Africa it may be 5-10% or higher, and in refugee camps and internally displaced populations rates have reached 20-30%. Previously vaccinated persons who become infected have less severe disease and significantly lower mortality. Measles still causes more than 100,000 deaths per year worldwide.
pitfalls: Patients are contagious before recognizable disease appears, which undermines isolation measures; nosocomial transmission in waiting rooms, hospitals, and physicians' offices is well recognized.

Clinical diagnosis is difficult during the prodrome, when the rash is attenuated by passively acquired antibody or prior immunization, when the rash is absent/delayed in immunocompromised or severely undernourished children, and in low-incidence regions.
Measles virus-specific IgM may be falsely negative if serum is obtained too early (within the first few days of rash onset).
Persons with impaired cellular immunity may not develop the characteristic rash, may develop giant cell pneumonitis, and have a high case-fatality rate.
There is no specific antiviral therapy; ribavirin benefit has not been conclusively demonstrated in trials.
The 1998 report hypothesizing an MMR-autism link was a misinterpreted temporal association, has been refuted by numerous studies, and was retracted - there is no causal link.
harrison.severityClassification: Harrison does not give a formal grading scale. Severity is driven by host and population factors: severe or fatal disease occurs in those with impaired/deficient T-lymphocyte (cellular) immunity and in malnourished/undernourished children (e.g., vitamin A deficiency), among whom the rash may be absent and giant cell pneumonitis and high case-fatality occur; pregnant women, immunocompromised persons, and infants <1 year are at risk of severe measles and are prioritized for immunoglobulin prophylaxis.
management: Supportive care with antipyretics, oral or intravenous rehydration and rest, as there is no specific licensed antiviral
Vitamin A supplementation for affected children to reduce morbidity and mortality
Treat secondary bacterial complications such as pneumonia and otitis media with appropriate antibacterials, which are not given routinely
Airborne and contact isolation to limit the high transmissibility, with statutory public-health notification
Post-exposure prophylaxis for susceptible contacts using MMR vaccine early after exposure, or human immunoglobulin where vaccine is contraindicated
Monitor for and manage complications including pneumonia, croup, encephalitis and dehydration
Consider ribavirin only in severe disease or immunocompromised patients, acknowledging limited evidence
Primary prevention through MMR immunisation of the population
